name: type-erasure
intent: Hold values of unrelated, non-inheriting types behind one non-templated interface - a type-erased wrapper - so that clients treat them uniformly through runtime dispatch, without forcing a common base class on the types themselves.
problem: A component must store, pass or return values whose concrete types it cannot know - callbacks, plugin-provided objects, the elements of a heterogeneous collection - and those types do share the behaviour the component needs, yet they have no common base class and cannot be edited to acquire one. Building the component as a template pushes the concrete type into every caller and rules out a single non-templated API or ABI boundary; demanding a base class means intrusive changes to types the component does not own.
context: Applies when the type set is open or third-party while the behaviour set is small and stable; when one non-templated type must cross a module, library or container boundary and hide the concrete types; and when polymorphic objects should be usable as values - copied, stored by value, returned - rather than through raw pointers. It is the runtime-dispatch counterpart of static polymorphism (templates, generics, concepts, CRTP) and complements it rather than replacing it.
benefits: One interface for unrelated types: callbacks, plugin objects and third-party classes become usable uniformly without a common base and without editing them (non-intrusive adaptation).
Open to new types: a new concrete type joins by being passed to the wrapper; neither the wrapper nor its clients change.

Removes the concrete type from the API surface: callers see one nominal type instead of a template parameter, which keeps a single ABI-visible type across library boundaries and prevents per-type template instantiation bloat.
Value semantics for polymorphic objects: a correctly implemented wrapper can be copied, stored in containers by value and returned, without exposing ownership pointers to clients.
Compile-time decoupling: only the binding site needs the concrete type and its header, so the rest of the program depends on the erased interface alone (shorter builds, fewer rebuilds).
Testability seam: production, fake and recording implementations are interchangeable without a shared base, because any type satisfying the operations can be bound to the interface.
tradeoffs: Runtime indirection and allocation: each operation goes through an indirect (virtual) call and each construction usually allocates unless an inline-storage optimisation applies - exactly the cost that templates, concepts and CRTP avoid.

The wrapper is open in types but closed in operations: adding one operation means editing the erased interface and every model that binds a type (or breaking every conformer in existential-based languages), so Visitor and Extension Object remain the right tools when operations, not types, are the axis of change.

Type information is discarded at the interface: equality, ordering, hashing, serialisation and downcasts must be re-exposed explicitly (clone, typeid, TypeId, TypeTest, any_cast) or deliberately given up; a naively erased wrapper supports none of them.

Errors move to the binding site: a concrete type missing an operation fails inside the wrapper's template constructor, often as a deep instantiation error, unless the language can state the constraint (concepts, protocol conformance) where the value is constructed.

Value semantics are not free: copying needs a virtual clone (allocation per copy) or shared state with copy-on-write, which reintroduces the sharing, lifetime and thread-safety questions the wrapper was meant to hide.

Hand-rolled wrappers are not ABI-stable across standard-library versions or compilers, so they are the wrong vehicle for a binary plugin boundary unless reduced to a C-style vtable plus context pointer.

participants.responsibility: The non-templated value type clients name; it owns the binding to a concrete value, directly or through a pointer/shared state, and forwards every operation to the erased interface.

The minimal set of operations the wrapper promises; in the hand-written form a hidden abstract class whose pure virtuals define the contract and whose virtual destructor and clone complete the object protocol.
A template instantiated once per concrete type that implements every Concept operation by forwarding to the stored value; it is the only place that knows the concrete type.
The unrelated, non-inheriting type that already provides the required behaviour; the pattern neither modifies it nor derives from it.

The template constructor or library factory that converts 'the concrete type is known here' into 'the rest of the program does not know it'; its constraints are where the implicit interface is checked.
The language-provided mechanism that makes the erased call work: vtable or witness table plus type descriptor, an itab for interfaces, or the dynamic object's own method table.

use_cases: Callback and listener registries that must hold lambdas, function pointers and functor objects from unrelated libraries behind one slot type (std::function, Action/Func, Runnable, a protocol existential).
Heterogeneous documents and scenes: an editor holds drawable, undoable or serialisable elements of unrelated types and iterates them uniformly.
Non-intrusive SDK boundaries: one opaque handle type (AnyView, AnyPublisher, AnySequence, boost::any, Box<dyn Error>) exposed across a module boundary so callers never see implementation types.
Testability seams: inject an erased collaborator (clock, logger, transport) so production and test implementations are interchangeable without sharing a base class.
Dynamic APIs and containers: attribute or configuration maps (std::any, object, Any, MessagePack-style values) and DI containers storing arbitrary services.
Bridging static and dynamic code: passing function objects through a C API (a qsort-style comparison callback) where the concrete callback type cannot be expressed.

Go I/O plumbing: net/http models Response.Body as an io.ReadCloser assembled from unrelated readers, and io.MultiReader / io.NopCloser compose any type with Read/Write/Close - files, sockets, gzip streams - behind the io interfaces without any shared base.

Swift boxed protocol types: an API or view tree holds [any Shape] existentials so unrelated conforming structs and classes mix in one collection across a module boundary, with the concrete type hidden behind the protocol witness table.

Rust heterogeneous components: a Screen holds Vec<Box<dyn Draw>> so Button and Image - unrelated types with no common base - coexist in one container and dispatch through a vtable, where a generic Vec<T> could carry only one concrete type.
avoid_when: The concrete type set is closed and known at compile time: a sealed hierarchy with exhaustive matching, a discriminated union or plain generics is simpler, allocation-free and statically checked.
A common base class already exists or can be introduced: ordinary inheritance or a Strategy reference keeps type information (downcasts, equality) that erasure would discard.
All types are known at the call site and code bloat is not an issue: templates, generics or CRTP give the same uniformity with zero indirection, so the erased layer buys nothing.
Operations are the axis of change: every new operation would have to be added to the erased interface and every bound model, so Visitor or Extension Object fits better.
One call site binds one concrete type: a plain function parameter or interface reference is enough; the wrapper is ceremony.
Values must be serialised, compared structurally or persisted across the boundary: erasure discards the type and usually the schema, so keep the typed representation.
anti_patterns: "Any/object soup": erasing to the universal type (std::any, Object, any) and casting back at every use - each type error becomes a runtime failure and the shared behaviour the pattern exists for is never stated.
Hand-rolling a wrapper for one known concrete type, or for a set that is closed and known at compile time - the indirection, allocation and clone cost buy no openness.
Erasing across a binary plugin boundary with a template-based wrapper: std::function's layout is not standardised, so mixed standard libraries corrupt the call instead of failing to compile.
Erasing a collaborator only to dodge a header dependency that deserves an explicit interface - hiding a real dependency inversion behind an opaque box.
Making the wrapper non-copyable and then sharing one instance between owners to compensate, reintroducing the lifetime and thread-safety problems the value-semantic form avoids.
Growing the erased interface until every caller's need is a method: the concept becomes a god interface, substitutability collapses and every model must implement everything.
design_principles: Program to an interface, but let the interface be non-intrusive: adaptation happens outside the concrete type (external polymorphism), so third-party and legacy types participate unchanged.
Separate binding from use: the concrete type is known only in the binding constructor, and all later code depends on the erased interface.
Invert dependencies at compile time: the interface owner includes no concrete-type headers, and concrete types do not derive from the wrapper.
Apply open/closed along the type axis: open for new types, closed for new operations - and make that closure an explicit decision, because Visitor or Extension Object owns the other axis.
Treat value semantics as a design tool: a polymorphic type that behaves like a regular value composes with containers and algorithms without pointer protocols.
Segregate the interface: the concept carries only the operations clients need, because every extra operation shrinks the set of types that can be bound.
best_practices: Start from the behaviour clients need, not from the types: define the smallest concept (one or two operations) and let the wrapper expose exactly that.

Prefer the erasure the language already provides - std::function/std::any, Action/Func, any P, dyn Trait, Protocol or duck typing - and hand-roll the Concept/Model wrapper only when the behaviour set is not covered.

Decide the object protocol explicitly: virtual destructor or type-erased deleter, clone when copies are allowed, move semantics, and a defined empty state (bad_function_call, Option, panic) instead of undefined behaviour.
Keep every Model<T> final and private to the wrapper so the concrete type never enters the public API and the compiler can devirtualise where the type is known.

Check the implicit interface where the concrete type is known - a concept/requires clause, protocol conformance or a static_assert in the constructor - so failures are reported at the binding site with a readable message.
Keep the binding constructor in the header but the erased calls out-of-line where possible, to limit template instantiation and rebuild cost.
Measure before adopting on a hot path: the wrapper costs at least one indirect call and often an allocation, and a closed type set is served better by a variant or enum dispatch.
Reduce the wrapper to a C-style table of function pointers plus a void* context and a destroy callback when it must cross a shared-library or plugin boundary.
sources: Cleeland, Schmidt & Harrison, External Polymorphism - An Object Structural Pattern for Transparently Extending C++ Concrete Data Types, PLoP 1996 (Pattern Languages of Program Design 3) - the origin of non-intrusive runtime polymorphism over unrelated types.
